essays.harness: Claude Code subagent, one essay per context
essays.text:
I think students would benefit from having distance learning as an option, but only as an option, not as the way school normally works. There are some situations where being able to attend class from home actually saves a student's whole semester, and there are other situations where it would just let people disappear. So my position is that schools should offer it, but they should be honest about who it works for.

The biggest reason I think it helps is that not every student can physically get to school every day. My cousin broke his leg in a soccer game in November and he was out for almost six weeks. He got a folder of worksheets sent home and that was it. He came back and he was so far behind in geometry that he basically never caught up, and he ended up having to retake it in summer school. If his school had let him log into his classes on a video call, he would have heard the teacher explain the proofs, he could have asked why he got something wrong, and he would have still been part of the class instead of just a name on the attendance sheet. That is not a small thing. Six weeks is a lot of math. There are also kids who have long term illnesses, or who are in and out of the hospital, or who have anxiety so bad that walking into a cafeteria is genuinely impossible for them. For those students distance learning isn't a convenience, it's the difference between graduating and not graduating.

Another reason is that it can give students access to classes their school doesn't have. My school only offers Spanish and French. If somebody wants to take Japanese or an AP class that only has four interested students, the school says no because it can't justify paying a teacher for four kids. But if those four kids could join a video class with students from three other schools in the district, suddenly it works. Small schools and rural schools especially get shortchanged on what they can offer, and this is a pretty direct fix.

But I don't think it should replace normal school, and I say that as somebody who did it during the pandemic and watched it go badly for a lot of people, including me sometimes. When I was on video calls I had my phone right there the whole time. I would have the class open in one window and be scrolling in another and I could tell myself I was paying attention, but I wasn't. Nobody could see me, half the class had their cameras off, and a teacher cannot tell that you are lost when all they can see is a black square with your name on it. In person, my chemistry teacher could look at my face while she was explaining molarity and know immediately that I had no idea what was happening, and she would stop and do it again. On a screen she just kept going.

There is also the part people don't like to bring up, which is that school is where you learn to be around other people. I got better at group projects because I had to sit next to people I did not choose and figure it out. You don't learn that from a breakout room that everyone leaves early. And some students don't have a quiet place at home, or reliable internet, or a parent around during the day, so "attend from home" ends up meaning "watch a frozen video while your little brother yells." That makes the gap between students bigger, not smaller.

So overall I think the answer is that distance learning is a good tool and a bad default. Schools should have it ready and working, so that when a student breaks a leg or gets sick or wants a class that isn't offered, the option is already there instead of being scrambled together at the last minute. But the normal school day should still happen in a building with a teacher who can actually see you. The students who need it would really benefit from it, and that is reason enough to offer it, as long as it isn't treated as the easy answer for everybody.

I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, but only if it stays an option and not the whole way school works. Having the choice helps students who otherwise lose weeks of learning, and it lets some people learn in a way that actually fits them. Taking the choice away from everybody just because it does not work for everybody is not fair.

The biggest reason is that things happen to people. Last winter I got strep throat and was out for six school days. My teachers posted some assignments but a lot of what I missed was just the class itself, the explaining part, and I never really got that back. I ended up teaching myself a whole unit of geometry out of the book at my kitchen table and my grade showed it. If I could have logged in from my bed on the days I felt okay, I would have at least heard the lesson. There are also students at my school who miss way more than six days, people with serious health problems, or people who have to watch younger siblings, or people whose families move in the middle of the year. For them distance learning is not a convenience, it is the difference between passing and not passing.

Another reason is that some students honestly learn better at home. School is loud. In my fourth period there is a group of kids who talk the entire time and the teacher spends probably ten minutes of every class just getting people quiet. A student who gets distracted easily, or who has anxiety and freezes up when they have to sit in a room with thirty people, might get more done in one hour at their desk at home than in three hours at school. My cousin did online classes for a year and she said she liked being able to pause the recording and rewind it when she did not get something. You cannot rewind a teacher.

I know people argue that students will not actually do the work, and honestly that is a real thing. When we did remote days during a snow week, half my class had their cameras off and I am pretty sure at least a few of them were asleep. It is way easier to zone out when nobody can see you. But that is an argument for doing distance learning well, with attendance checks and teachers who actually call on people, not an argument for never doing it. Students zone out in the classroom too, they just do it with their eyes open.

The other argument is that you miss out on being around people, and I think that one is more serious. School is where I see my friends and where I learned how to work in a group with somebody I did not pick. If everybody stayed home all the time we would lose that, which is exactly why it should be a choice instead of the default.

So my position is that schools should offer distance learning, because for a lot of students it is the only way they get to keep learning when life gets in the way, and for some of them it is simply a better way to learn. It should not replace the building. It should be there for the people who need it.

I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, but I want to be careful about how I say that, because I don't mean school should become a website. I mean it should be an option, the way taking a bus or getting a ride is an option. Some students need it and right now a lot of schools act like the only real school is the one that happens inside the building between 7:45 and 2:30.

I'm not guessing about this. I did a year and change of school on a laptop at my kitchen table, and I know exactly how bad it can be. I slept through first period more times than I want to admit. My little brother basically stopped doing math for four months and nobody noticed until report cards. So when people say distance learning failed, I'm not going to pretend it didn't. But I think we're drawing the wrong lesson from it. What happened then was an emergency where every single student got thrown into the same system at the same time whether it fit them or not, with teachers who had three days to figure out how to do it. That's not a fair test of anything. That's like judging swimming lessons based on a shipwreck.

The real reason to offer it is that students' lives are not identical. There's a girl in my chemistry class who has some kind of chronic illness, I don't know the name of it, and she misses maybe two weeks a semester in chunks. She is not a bad student. She is a very good student who keeps falling into holes she then has to climb out of by emailing five teachers and hoping they answer. If she could log in on the days she physically can't get up and get dressed, she wouldn't be behind at all. Same with the kid on my street who works closing shifts at the restaurant his family owns, and the students who are in and out for medical stuff or court stuff or family stuff that nobody at school knows about.

There's also the plain issue of what a school can actually offer. My school is not big. We have one AP science, and if you want physics you take it online through the county already, which honestly proves my point, because nobody calls that distance learning, they just call it the schedule. Small and rural schools could give students access to classes they'd otherwise never see. A student in a town of two thousand people shouldn't be locked out of Mandarin or calculus because there aren't enough bodies to fill a classroom.

I do think there are real losses and I don't want to just wave at them. You cannot titrate a solution over Zoom. You can't really have the kind of argument we had in my English class about whether Gatsby is actually in love or just obsessed, where four people talk at once and someone gets mad, over a video call where everyone is muted and staring at their own face. And school is where a lot of people learn how to be around other people they didn't choose, which is most of adult life. Those things matter and they're the reason I'd fight anyone who wanted to make it the default.

But an option is not a default. Nobody is forced to take the bus. Let students who need it attend from home, keep the building open and full for everybody else, and stop pretending that the only students who count are the ones who can show up in person every single day.

Some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home by way of online or video conferencing. Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home? Take a position on this issue. Support your response with reasons and examples.

I think students would benefit from having distance learning as an option, but I want to be careful about that word "option," because I don't think it works as a replacement. As a choice a student can make when their situation calls for it, it's valuable. As the default way school happens, it falls apart, and I say that as somebody who lived through it.

My sophomore year we were remote for about four months. I'll be honest, the first two weeks felt great. I slept until 7:50 and logged on at 8. I ate lunch in my own kitchen instead of a cafeteria that smells like bleach and pizza. My grades actually went up at first, partly because a lot of assignments turned into "submit by midnight" instead of "hand it in now," and I work better at night anyway. So I'm not going to pretend distance learning is useless. For a certain kind of student, the flexibility is real.

But by month three it stopped working for most people I knew. Not because the technology failed, because the accountability did. In a classroom, if I zone out, Mr. Petrossian notices and says my name. On a video call, I could have my camera off and be doing literally anything. I did do literally anything, some days. Nobody is coming to get you, and it turns out that at seventeen a lot of us aren't ready to be the only person holding ourselves to a standard. There were kids in my AP Chem class who I'm pretty sure never turned their camera on the entire semester and just quietly disappeared. They weren't lazy. They just had nothing pulling them back.

There's also the part nobody wants to admit, which is that school is where you learn to be around people you didn't choose. I had to do a group project with a kid I could not stand and we had to figure it out anyway. That's a real skill. You can't get it through a screen where you can mute somebody. My younger cousin started high school remote and he's a junior now and he still talks to people like he's typing.

So why do I still say it should be offered? Because there are students for whom the building itself is the barrier. A girl I know has a chronic illness and misses probably thirty days a year. Under the old system she was just behind, permanently, catching up on borrowed notes. With a remote option she could actually attend from her bed on bad days. Students with serious anxiety, students who are caretakers for younger siblings, students taking a class their school doesn't even offer so they have to get it from a community college two towns over. For all of those people, distance learning isn't a lesser version of school. It's the only version that reaches them.

That's my position. Offer it, fund it properly so it isn't just a teacher pointing a laptop at a whiteboard, and let students and families choose it when it fits. But don't let districts use it as a cheap substitute for actual classrooms, because for most of us, most of the time, the classroom is doing work we don't notice until it's gone.
